beats.intro: Module one. [[sub]]A bond is a loan that can be traded. This module shows what it promises, and what protects the lender.
beats.loan: Companies and governments need money. [[a]]They borrow it from investors, through loans and bonds. [[b]]A loan is a private agreement, usually with a bank. A bond is more standard, so it is easier to trade. [[c]]In return, the lender receives interest, and gets the principal back at the end. [[d]]Those promised payments are why we call it fixed income.
beats.features: Every bond is described by a few features. [[f1]]The issuer, who is borrowing. [[f2]]The maturity, when the loan ends. [[f3]]The principal, also called par, or face value. [[f4]]The coupon rate, and how often it is paid. [[f5]]The seniority, which decides who is paid first. [[f6]]And contingency provisions, special rights that can change the bond. [[end]]Together, these features fix the bond's cash flows.
beats.cashflows: Here is a typical bond. A company issues a five year note, with a par value of three hundred million dollars, and a three point two percent coupon, paid every six months. [[t0]]At the start, investors hand over three hundred million. [[coupons]]Every six months, the issuer pays a coupon. The annual coupon is the coupon rate times par. Three point two percent of three hundred million is nine point six million a year. [[half]]Paid twice a year, that is four point eight million each time. [[last]]At maturity, after ten payments, the issuer pays the last coupon plus the principal. Three hundred four point eight million.
beats.seniority: What if the issuer fails? [[pot]]Suppose its assets are sold for one hundred. [[claims]]Debt has a ranking. Senior secured lenders, backed by collateral, come first. Then senior unsecured. Then junior, or subordinated. [[pay]]The money flows down the line. Forty pays the secured claim in full. Fifty pays the unsecured claim in full. [[junior]]Only ten is left for a junior claim of sixty. [[note]]Lower seniority means more loss, so those investors demand a higher yield.
beats.contingency: Some bonds carry options. [[call]]A callable bond lets the issuer repay early, which helps the issuer when rates fall. [[put]]A putable bond lets the investor sell it back to the issuer, which helps the investor. [[conv]]A convertible bond lets the investor swap it for shares. [[note]]Whoever holds the option gains, so the bond's yield adjusts to pay for it.
beats.yield: An investor earns two things from a bond. [[inc]]The coupons, and [[chg]]any change in the bond's price. The yield summarizes this return. [[curve]]Take a five year bond with a three point two percent coupon. At a yield of three point two percent, its price equals par, one hundred. [[up]]If yields rise, the price falls. [[down]]If yields fall, the price rises. [[inv]]Price and yield move in opposite directions.
beats.curve: Yields also depend on maturity. [[a]]The yield curve plots yield against time to maturity. [[b]]Usually, longer bonds pay higher yields, so the curve slopes upward. [[c]]Investors are asking for more compensation for lending longer.
beats.credit: Credit risk is the risk that the issuer does not pay in full and on time. [[ladder]]The less credit risk, the lower the yield. A government bond backed by taxes sits low. A weaker corporate borrower sits high. [[src]]Credit quality depends on the source of repayment. Taxes and fiscal power for governments, operating cash flow for companies, and the asset pool for securitized debt. [[coll]]Collateral and seniority add protection, and so does the issuer's willingness to pay.
beats.indenture: The bond's legal contract is called the indenture. [[cov]]It contains covenants, which are legally enforceable promises. [[aff]]Affirmative covenants say what the issuer must do. Pay on time, keep insurance, and publish financial statements. [[neg]]Negative covenants say what the issuer must not do. Take on too much extra debt, or sell key assets. [[pari]]A pari passu clause puts the bond on equal footing with the issuer's other senior debt.
beats.wrap: Let's recap. [[w1]]A bond promises coupons, and the return of par at maturity. [[w2]]Issuer, maturity, par, coupon, seniority and options define it. [[w3]]Price and yield move in opposite directions, and weaker credit means a higher yield. [[w4]]The indenture and its covenants protect the lender.
